summary: Introduces use cases for Time-Variant Routing, where routing computations take into account scheduled or time-based changes in a network. Such planning could improve convergence and performance, for example in networks whose links come and go predictably.

eli5.summary: Some network links are only available at certain times, like a bus that runs on a schedule. This describes why routers should plan using the timetable instead of finding out when the bus is gone.

questions: use cases for scheduled network changes in routing
tvr use cases for scheduled network changes
subtitle: Routing optimization when network changes occur at predictable times.

tldr.problem: Networks with predictable scheduled changes (like satellites orbiting, energy-harvesting nodes, mobile networks with time-of-use pricing) do not leverage knowledge of when links will come and go. Traditional routing protocols treat such changes as disruptions rather than planning opportunities.
tldr.mechanism: Time-Variant Routing (TVR) allows routing computations to consider scheduled or predictable changes to network topology over time, selecting paths that optimize for when links are available. Managers configure policies based on energy patterns, mobility predictions, or cost schedules.
tldr.outcome: Three categories of use cases benefit: Resource Preservation (nodes power on/off based on energy or thermal constraints), Operating Efficiency (routes chosen based on time-of-use costs), and Dynamic Reachability (mobility of satellites or vessels is predictable). This prevents unnecessary routing convergence delays.

facts.label: Routing impacts
facts.value: Reduces convergence time, enables offline route planning

today: RFC 9657 is an Informational RFC documenting use cases that motivate Time-Variant Routing research and standardization. TVR is still an emerging concept without widely deployed standards, though research continues in the IETF.

sections.title: Why Networks Change Predictably
sections.content:
Growing numbers of networks have expected topology changes built into their design. These changes are not failures; they are normal operations. Examples include mobile nodes like unmanned aerial vehicles or spacecraft constellations, networks harvesting energy from sun or wind (with links restricted to daylight hours), and networks designed for green computing (with intentionally scheduled energy usage).

Traditional routing protocols (like OSPF or ISIS) treat topology changes as errors to be recovered from, triggering expensive flooding and reconvergence across the network. In challenged networks where links go down and come up in predictable patterns, this behavior wastes bandwidth and processing time. Instead, routers could pre-compute paths knowing when changes will occur.

The TVR use cases in this document define three categories where route computation might beneficially take time into account. Each use case includes assumptions about the network and a description of routing impacts and real-world examples.
sections.eli5: Imagine a town where the only bridge closes every night. A smart router would know 'use the bridge from 6 AM to 6 PM' instead of being surprised when it closes at 6:01 PM.

sections.title: Resource Preservation: Nodes with Scheduled Power
sections.content:
Resource-constrained nodes often operate under predictable power cycles. Solar-powered sensors accumulate charge during the day and must turn off their radios to conserve power at night. Thermal constraints might require that node processors are powered down when temperature rises above safe levels. Local storage limitations force periodic transmission windows.

TVR enables nodes to communicate their expected availability, so remote nodes can route data through them only during predictable active windows. The network learns: 'Node 2 has power on Tuesdays from 8 AM to 10 AM,' and plans accordingly rather than attempting delivery at 2 PM and failing.

The use case assumes: (1) known resource expenditures (nodes understand power/thermal budgets), (2) predictable resource accumulation (like solar recharge at dawn), and (3) consistent cost functions (behavior is deterministic enough to plan).
sections.eli5: A solar-powered sensor knows it will have enough energy to send messages in the morning but must sleep in the evening. Routers can plan to reach it in the morning instead of trying at night.

sections.title: Operating Efficiency: Time-Based Cost Optimization
sections.content:
Networks operating over infrastructure with time-of-use pricing (like cellular networks with peak/off-peak rates or power grids with variable pricing) can optimize costs if they know when prices change. Nodes can delay non-critical traffic until rates drop, or route through cheaper paths during low-cost windows.

One example is a cellular network where many schedulable tasks (nightly backups, software updates, log synchronization) already expect to run at specific times. A second example, a 'tidal network,' has predictable traffic surges during business hours. Energy-saving methods can selectively power down network links during low-traffic times, creating a known schedule that TVR can use.

The use case assumes: (1) cost measurability (per-bit cost or per-kilowatt cost is known), (2) cost predictability (cost changes are communicated in advance), (3) cost persistence (prices stay stable long enough for behavior adjustment), and (4) cost magnitude (savings are large enough to justify routing based on time).
sections.eli5: Electricity is cheaper in the evening than during the day. A smart network might wait until evening to send large file transfers when the cost is lower.

sections.title: Dynamic Reachability: Mobile Nodes with Predictable Paths
sections.content:
Mobile platforms (satellites, aircraft, ships) follow deterministic or semi-deterministic paths. A Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellation follows predictable orbital mechanics; each spacecraft is in view of a ground station for only a few minutes per pass, and engineers can compute when that pass occurs. This reachability is predictable enough for routers to plan when adjacencies will expire or resume.

Spacecraft in a 'string of pearls' configuration maintain consistent inter-satellite links because of stable orbital mechanics, but links to ground stations come and go on a predictable schedule. Vessels with fixed routes (ferries, commercial ships) or aircraft following flight plans have similarly predictable motion.

The use case assumes: (1) path predictability (node mobility is known or can be predicted), and (2) environmental knowledge (duration of connectivity loss due to storms, tunnels, or horizon effects is calculable).
sections.eli5: A satellite orbiting Earth passes over the same ground station at the same time each day. A router can plan 'send to the ground station via Satellite 3 between 2:15 PM and 2:22 PM' because it knows that orbit.

sections.title: Security and Synchronization
sections.content:
The use of time-based routing introduces security considerations beyond traditional routing. Time synchronization is critical: if network clocks are not synchronized, TVR schedules become unreliable, and nodes may believe adjacencies are available when they are not (or unavailable when they are). Unauthorized changes to network clocks could cause routes to fail or create denial-of-service conditions.

TVR implementations should employ time-based validation and revocation strategies to ensure that route policies expire or update at appropriate times. The document does not define specific mechanisms but notes that security solutions should be addressed in TVR schedule definitions or through protocol extensions using TVR schedules.
sections.eli5: If clocks are wrong, routers might think a link exists when it does not. Everyone needs to agree on what time it is.
